title: Chennai Air Worsens Sharply on Diwali as Four Areas Cross AQI 300
excerpt: Valasaravakkam hit 343 and the CPCB city average rose to 199 from 142 a year earlier — the steepest rise among major cities — despite a two-window firecracker rule that was widely ignored.
body:
• Chennai's air deteriorated sharply over Diwali: four neighbourhoods crossed AQI 300 into the 'very poor' band, led by Valasaravakkam at 343, Nungambakkam at 332, Sowcarpet at 311 and T. Nagar at 306, NDTV reported.
  • On the Central Pollution Control Board's 24-hour city average to 4 p.m. on November 9, Chennai's AQI rose to 199 from 142 last Diwali — the steepest rise among 10 major cities, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.
  • Tamil Nadu's statewide average AQI ticked up to 168.97 in 2026 from 161.69 in 2025, with 25 of 39 monitoring stations recording an increase.
  • Firecrackers were permitted only in two one-hour windows — 6–7 a.m. and 7–8 p.m. — but NDTV reported large-scale disregard of the windows across the city.

Chennai's air quality deteriorated sharply over Diwali, pushing major commercial and residential hubs into the 'very poor' category on Sunday, NDTV reported. Valasaravakkam, a dense residential pocket in southwest Chennai, recorded the highest reading in the city at an AQI of 343, followed by Nungambakkam at 332, Sowcarpet at 311 and T. Nagar at 306.

Two ways of counting, one direction

Citywide averages tell the same story on a different scale. City-wise data from the Central Pollution Control Board, capturing the average AQI over 24 hours to 4 p.m. on November 9, put Chennai at 199, up from 142 in Diwali 2025 — a deterioration of 57 points and, among the 10 major cities tracked, the steepest rise, The Hindu BusinessLine reported. IANS, reporting an earlier snapshot, put the city's average at 159, with Royapuram the worst-affected locality at 238, followed by Perungudi at 175, Manali at 168, Kodungaiyur at 166 and Arumbakkam at 165. Under the CPCB scale, 101–200 is 'moderate', 201–300 is 'poor' and 301–400 is 'very poor'.

Across Tamil Nadu, the state's average AQI ticked up to 168.97 in 2026 from 161.69 in 2025 and 143.46 in 2024, with 25 out of 39 monitoring stations recording an increase, NDTV reported. Kancheepuram recorded 250, Trichy 240, Tiruppur 223 and Thanjavur 210, while Nagapattinam improved to a satisfactory 71, alongside improvements in Cuddalore, Thoothukudi and Krishnagiri. Delhi's AQI, by comparison, improved marginally from 351 last Diwali to 344 this year, though it remained 'very poor'; Patna worsened from 226 to 280 and Bengaluru from 97 to 133.

Noise rose too, and the windows were ignored

The state government had permitted bursting crackers only from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. to 8 p.m., and ran awareness campaigns — but there was large-scale disregard for the regulations amid poor enforcement, with firecrackers fired throughout the day, NDTV reported. The arithmetic average Deepavali noise level rose from 75.70 dB(A) in 2025 to 76.73 dB(A) in 2026, led by Valasaravakkam at 88.6 dB(A). Intermittent rain during the festivities did little to hold pollution down, IANS reported.

The readings carry a familiar argument. Before the festival, former BJP leader K. Annamalai urged citizens to buy and burst crackers, noting the industry directly employs 3 lakh people and indirectly supports another 5 lakh workers in Sivakasi: "When we buy firecrackers, we are helping someone put food on the table." Environmental group Poovulagin Nanbargal countered that safety conditions were systematically flouted. For residents, the practical exposure is immediate: elevated pollution can cause breathing discomfort, particularly among children, older people and those with asthma or other respiratory conditions, IANS noted.
